- i'm the reporter. - i would like to speak about the two files of mrs sehnalová and myself. the files are very interwoven. we have, in fact, on the one hand, the report by mrs sehnalová on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the type-approval requirements for the deployment of the ecall in-vehicle system, and on the other hand, my report on the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council on the introduction of an interoperable ecall throughout the european union. this decision obliges member states to have their infrastructure ready in time to receive the 112 ecalls. i therefore fully support the european commission's proposal to make ecall mandatory for all new vehicles from 1 october 2015. the fact that today less than 1% of vehicles in the european union are fitted with the system shows that the voluntary approach was not really a success. automated calls can effectively lead to a faster response by the emergency services. it also means a reduction in the number of deaths and serious injuries, as every minute can be vital in saving lives. in belgium, it could lead to a reduction in the number of road deaths by about 70 per year. in my report i have made a number of specific points: the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the 112 service is available in the member states, and that the psaps, the central receiving centres, are also available in the member states. the member states should therefore only adapt those systems so that they can also receive the 112 ecalls. it also explicitly gives member states the possibility to filter, to distinguish non-urgent from urgent ecalls. that certainly improves the efficiency of the system. it is important to make european citizens aware of the benefits of this system; member states should raise awareness among their citizens. the type-approval directive specifies the requirements to be met by the 112-ecall system. i can support mrs sehnalová's report in its broad outline, as adopted by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to participate in the work of the european parliament. it's already in a number of cars, and it's already been introduced by a number of manufacturers. drivers wishing to have such a system in their car should therefore also be able to choose additional applications for the ecall system. the report does make it clear - and this is important - that the 112 system is a public and basic system available to everyone. in this way, i think we have found a good compromise between the two systems, the existing and the new. there has also been a lot of discussion about data protection and privacy. i think that we in the liberal group have a real interest in fully defending and safeguarding the privacy of individuals. of course, to make that choice in a good way, one must know what the ecall system does. the ecall system is a sleeping system that only sends a signal when an accident occurs. it only contains information on the last three times and the last three positions of the driver, so that the emergency services can be alerted very quickly to the location of the vehicle and the direction in which it was moving. in addition, the system today - and this is very important to mention - also falls within the existing system of european data protection legislation. i understand the concern and also that we must always strike a balance between the data people provide to obtain a service and the privacy of the data, but i think that in this case the balance is right and we can use this system with confidence. i therefore call on everyone to support the report tomorrow by a very large majority and to send a very strong signal to the council and our citizens as a parliament that we want to see this system introduced as soon as possible and that we give absolute priority to road safety. we want to do everything we can to reduce the number of road deaths.

a system that makes it possible for emergency services to arrive on the scene more quickly after an accident is, of course, a good thing. but the problem is that the ecall system opens the door wide to all kinds of abuses. the system allows third parties to request almost any information about our cars and the use made of those cars. where we go, how often we go, how long we stay, how fast we drive, and so on. it's not just the government that can be an unwanted bystander, because criminals can also hack into the system, which in any case has the potential to steal cars, or worse, to disable or activate certain features of those cars. and i'm not hearing satisfactory answers to all these concerns. the system should not be made mandatory. the car has long been a symbol of freedom. the ecall system could change this in a very profound way in the future.

in writing. in the event of an accident, your car's ecall system will automatically dial 112. all new vehicles sold in the european union from october 2015 will be fitted with it. the aim is to save 2500 lives a year across europe, cut the response time in half and save 26 billion euros in the event of a major accident. the main benefit of the system is that it immediately alerts the emergency services to the precise location of the accident. this will reduce the time taken for emergency services to arrive by about 50% in rural areas and by 40% in urban areas. the eu's ecall could save up to 2500 lives a year in the eu and also significantly reduce the severity of injuries in 15% of cases. the system could save 26 billion euros annually. faster detection of the accident allows for faster treatment of victims (thus lower medical costs) and of road traffic (reducing the colossal costs of traffic jams). in summary, today's decision should reduce road deaths. this is far from a luxury when you consider that nearly 30,000 people die every year on european macadam.

in writing. on 13 june 2013, the european commission adopted two proposals to equip all new cars with an ecall system by october 2015, which will automatically call the emergency services (the single european emergency call number 112) in the event of a serious accident. even if passengers are unable to speak, ecall creates a voice link with the nearest emergency call centre and sends a distress call. the system allows for language-free calls and should make a significant contribution to reducing the number of road deaths and injuries in europe, by reducing the response times of emergency services. it is estimated that 2,500 lives could be saved annually; in addition, the severity of many injuries could be considerably reduced. the ecall system improves incident management while reducing traffic problems caused by accidents and the likelihood of secondary accidents. while private emergency call services are already installed in 0.7%[nbsp ] of european cars, none of them offer eu-wide coverage.

in writing. value added tax (vat) in the european union is a general consumption tax, broadly based, calculated on the value added of all commercial activities, which include the production and distribution of goods and the provision of services, with a few exceptions. vat is not normally charged on goods sold for export or for the supply of services. it does, however, apply to imports in order to put eu producers on an equal footing with their competitors on the internal market, namely suppliers of goods and services imported from third countries. vat is an indirect tax which is ultimately borne by the final consumer. it is levied as a percentage of the price paid by the buyer to the seller and is collected in the form of partial payments, each taxable person (whether registered for vat or self-employed) deducting from the vat he has collected the amount of tax he has already paid to other taxable persons on purchases made for the purposes of his business activities. this mechanism ensures tax neutrality, regardless of the number of transactions.
in writing. decision 2009/831/ec sets out the reasons for the adoption of specific measures, in particular the small size and fragmentation of agricultural holdings and their low level of mechanisation. in addition, the transport to the islands of certain raw materials and packaging materials which are not produced locally involves additional costs compared to the simple transport of finished products. transport and installation of equipment to these remote island regions adds to the extra costs. finally, the producers concerned also have to bear the general additional costs for the local economy, in particular in terms of labour and energy supply. the 75% reduction is not more than is necessary to offset the additional costs incurred by the operators concerned due to the special characteristics of the outermost regions of madeira and the azores mentioned above. as the tax advantage is limited to what is strictly necessary to offset the additional costs and the volumes involved remain modest, the measure does not undermine the integrity and coherence of the union legal order. moreover, the tax advantage is limited to consumption in the regions concerned.
in writing. decision 2004/162/ec sets out the reasons for the adoption of these specific measures: remoteness, insularity, small market size and underdeveloped exports, difficult terrain and climate, economic dependence on a small number of products, and even sometimes natural phenomena such as cyclones, volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. the remoteness of these regions and their dependence on air and sea transport, as well as their dependence on energy and raw materials, have an impact on production costs. the combination of all these disadvantages leads to an increase in the cost of locally produced goods, so that without specific measures they would not be able to compete with goods produced elsewhere. if local products are not competitive, it will be impossible to maintain local production, with the harmful consequences for the employment of the people living in these regions. the specific measures contained in decision 2004/162/ec were therefore designed to strengthen the local industry by improving its competitiveness.

in writing. as adopted in committee, this proposal lays down the rules for the opening of the market for rail passenger services. it preserves the integrated structures which it makes compatible with an open market, where several actors operate on the network. market access may be limited if the viability of certain public services is compromised. this leaves countries free to choose the organisation of their network and to revert at any time to a more integrated model. the compromise text gives priority to the separation of financial flows: the infrastructure manager's revenues must be reinvested in the sector and loans between entities of a holding structure must be supervised by the regulatory body. despite the strict separation of accounts, cooperation with other entities of the holding company remains possible, as long as it is covered by a contract in accordance with the prevailing market behaviour. the rapporteur intends to table a series of amendments in plenary to improve the collaboration between infrastructure managers and railway undertakings in the context of the integration of structures, provided that strict conditions of non-discrimination and transparency are applied, similar to those of separate structures.

in writing. over the last decade, the eu rail market has been profoundly changed, in a progressive manner, by the introduction of three railway legislative packages designed to open up national markets and increase the competitiveness and interoperability of railways at eu level, while maintaining a high level of safety. however, the modal share of rail in intra-eu transport remains modest. despite these three legislative packages, the european railway sector still faces problems such as obstacles to competition, discrimination and the absence of a liberalised, dynamic and business-friendly environment. today, there are too many national rules, with procedures and standards that lack transparency.
in writing. the purpose of this proposal is to repeal regulation (eec) no 1192/69, and therefore the text of the regulation itself cannot be amended. while in all previous railway packages as presented by the commission and then adopted and transposed by the member states, the aim was to extend rights and obligations to all new entrants to the sector and thus to open up the railway market, here the commission proposes to remedy any discrimination between undertakings in the sector, not by making an appropriate recast, as in the case of other legislative texts, but by simply deleting the text, i.e. by repealing the regulation.
in writing. with a strong growth in air traffic forecast for 2030, preventive aviation safety measures should be strengthened to ensure that the number of air accidents does not follow the curve of traffic growth. while the effectiveness of accident investigation systems in the european union is commendable, considerable efforts are now required in the proactive collection and analysis of events. while accident investigations are concerned with analysing the causes of a crash, the event reporting system aims to identify incidents which, if not known and corrected, could contribute to a disaster. this regulation aims to strengthen and deepen the proactive accident prevention system through analysis and rapid exchange of information, thereby contributing to the achievement of the objectives set out in the 2011 transport white paper. the only way to improve safety is to have a system that can clearly identify any failures and take preventive or corrective measures quickly. as this whole proactive system is based on the spontaneous reporting of events by airline employees, it is essential to ensure that an environment of trust, a 'just culture', is established.
in writing. the ecall service will significantly reduce the number of road traffic fatalities across the european union. with this early warning system, we will not only reduce the severity of injuries but also save more lives. as regards the use of the data to be collected, i have paid particular attention to their protection. the deployment of the ecall system should be preceded by an awareness-raising campaign to explain to union citizens the benefits of this new system and the guarantees it offers in terms of data protection.
in writing. on 13 june 2013, the european commission adopted two proposals to equip all new cars with an ecall system by october 2015, which will automatically call the emergency services (the single european emergency call number 112) in the event of a serious accident. even if passengers are unable to speak, ecall creates a voice link with the nearest emergency call centre and sends a distress call. the system, which allows for calls without language problems, should make a significant contribution to reducing the number of deaths and injuries on european roads, by reducing the response times of emergency services. it is estimated that 2,500 lives could be saved annually; in addition, the severity of many injuries could be reduced considerably. the ecall system improves incident management while reducing traffic problems caused by accidents and the likelihood of secondary accidents. while private emergency call services are already available in 0.7% of european cars, none of them offer eu-wide coverage.
in writing. amendments are to be made to directive 2002/92/ec of the european parliament and of the council. it is therefore proposed to revise this directive. since the main purpose and object of this directive is to harmonise national provisions in the above-mentioned field, it should be based on articles 53 (1) and 62 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the form of a directive is appropriate because it allows, if necessary, an adaptation of the implementing measures to any specificity of the market or the particular legal system of a member state. this directive is based on article 53 (1) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, since its purpose is to coordinate national rules governing access to the activity of insurance and reinsurance intermediation.

in writing. the health for growth programme has an overall budget of €446 million for the period 2014-2020, i.e. more than €60 million per year. it aims to focus on the main areas where eu action can bring real added value in the health sector. it is part of the europe 2020 strategy and aims to encourage innovation in healthcare, ensure its sustainability and improve the well-being of european citizens. this funding complements a number of health-related measures through the structural funds and the framework programme for research and innovation 2014-2020. compared to the previous period (2007-2013), this programme has seen an increase of 5.7%. potential applicants for funding will be national authorities, public and private bodies, international organisations and non-governmental organisations through co-financing. it is essential that the procedures and access to these budgets are as simple as possible so that they can be better used by member states and health professionals.

in writing. in the digital age, the provision of information and services online is increasing. as a result, the number of public and private sector websites is increasing rapidly. there are now 761,000 public sector websites that already offer access to information and services only. however, less than 10% of websites in the european union currently meet web accessibility standards. the union market for web accessibility is made up of more than 175[nbsp ]000 companies. the turnover generated by the approximately one million people working in the web development industry is estimated at eur 144 billion. accessibility of the web is essential, as it allows everyone, including people with disabilities, to use websites. public sector bodies and all other entities providing basic services to the public need to adopt inclusive web accessibility practices in order to fulfil their responsibilities towards all citizens.

in writing. this report on prostitution and sexual exploitation is based on the guidelines for victims of violence and human trafficking. according to various reports, there are some 40 to 42 million people engaged in prostitution worldwide, and about 96 percent of those in prostitution are women. the first eurostat report with official prostitution data was published in april 2013. it focused on human trafficking in the eu between 2008 and 2010. it indicated that 62% of trafficked women were victims of sexual exploitation and that they were largely from eu countries. prostitution is also linked to organized crime, the second largest after drug trafficking, and according to the havoscope website, it generates an estimated $186 billion in annual revenue worldwide.
in writing. countries that have long been importers of minerals, such as the united states, japan and european countries, face increasing competition for access to strategic mineral resources and security of supply. this situation gives developing countries the opportunity to benefit from their natural resources. while the unprecedented global demand for minerals and other natural resources represents a unique opportunity to enable mining to contribute to sustainable development, it also poses significant challenges for developing countries. the exploitation of high-value natural resources such as oil, gas, minerals and timber is a major source of conflict worldwide, especially in a context of increasing competition for access to increasingly scarce renewable resources such as land and water. environmental degradation, population growth and climate change are further exacerbating this situation. the poor management of land and natural resources contributes to new conflicts and hinders the peaceful resolution of existing conflicts.

the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, europe is an idea of freedom, peace, solidarity and shared prosperity better than anywhere else in the world. these values are politically, but above all legally, anchored in the european treaties. it is a matter of adhering to these values and to the treaties which enshrine the fundamental rights of all european citizens. when a country joins the european union, it takes a legal commitment to respect the texts that enshrine our common values. we are witnessing in all the countries of the european union violations of the values, principles and legislation which must guarantee the rule of law and respect for the values of humanity and universality which characterize our institutions and our texts. we must admit that there are still too many places in europe and too many cases of serious breaches of the rules to which all the states subscribed in order to join the european union. there are too many examples where eu member states trivialize or ignore the rights of the disabled, migrants, roma, trade unions, the right to strike, the right to associate, to assemble, the protection of privacy, the independence of the media, the judiciary, the army, and so on. if europe is to be a moral force that intends to influence the world for the better, it must be severe and rigorous with itself. we europeans are right to fight for democracy, the rule of law, the impartiality of public authority, the protection of privacy and individual and collective rights everywhere in the world. but we will do so with all the more effectiveness if we are credible. i repeat, by joining the european union, the member states are joining the legislative acts which guarantee the exercise of these values. unfortunately, too often today some people forget what they committed themselves to yesterday. the report we are presenting to you strengthens the human rights policy based on the present treaties and opens up a reflection for a future revision of the treaties. nothing prevents the member states today from completing the process of accession of the european union to the european convention on human rights, from completing the process of accession of the european union to the european social charter, from acceding to the conventions of the council of europe on human rights, from setting up the copenhagen mechanism under the moral aegis of a committee of wise men. this would give member states the guarantee of being treated equally, fairly, transparently and objectively, on the one hand, and the citizen of being respected in his fundamental rights. the second pillar of the institutional part of this report calls for a reflection on the necessary amendments to the treaties. but we claim that the essential can already be achieved on the basis of the existing treaties. the adoption of this report will be a major step forward in ensuring better protection for our citizens. these fundamental rights and european values cannot be treated as separate and circumvented subjects. they must be applied consistently and horizontally. the report calls for the integration of ambitious policies and action programmes to guarantee fundamental rights, including the adoption of an anti-discrimination directive. we have paid particular attention to ensuring the application of article[nbsp ]2 of the treaty, to maintaining the horizontal approach, to protecting minorities and all citizens in a vulnerable position, to protecting witnesses who dare to denounce illegal situations, to affirming the fundamental right to privacy and to upholding the secularism and impartiality of the state. finally, i would like to make one last appeal to the members who are presenting an alternative resolution. i fully respect your views, ladies and gentlemen, but your draft is a totally watered-down version of my report. you're draining it of the most basic elements. you prefer a safe approach, which, in some respects, frankly, worries me. you propose to delete many references which, however, violate fundamental rights, including references to the european social charter, european history and the genesis of the european project, the copenhagen mechanism, the problem of overcrowding in prisons, the suicide rate within the lgbt community, secularism and the strict separation of religion and state.

in writing. to ensure the effectiveness of the single market for the benefit of citizens and businesses, it is essential to improve the information that citizens and businesses have access to regarding their rights in the single market and the rules in force in different member states, as well as to offer them the necessary assistance in solving cross-border problems. these objectives have been a priority for parliament for several years. solvit as a tool has achieved tangible results and has proven its usefulness and value for the single market. nevertheless, there is still considerable room for improvement in giving citizens and businesses the opportunity to enjoy their rights in the single market through solvit and other measures. many examples of superficial, late or incorrect implementation and of national provisions contrary to eu legislation can be and are being discovered through solvit files. solvit is often the body to which citizens and businesses turn to draw the attention of the authorities to certain malfunctions. solvit therefore has considerable potential to improve the functioning of the single market as a whole and much more action is needed to use this knowledge and observations to correct problems.
in writing. efficient and impartial justice is based primarily on the ability to obtain evidence. in the face of transnational crime in europe, it is necessary to facilitate it through a european approach and not confined to a purely national perspective. such a mechanism already exists in europe. however, due to its complexity and fragmentation, it is used very rarely, to the detriment of judicial efficiency. i therefore welcome this report, which seeks to strengthen such a mechanism, in particular through the principle of mutual recognition, coordination of investigations and respect for fundamental rights in criminal proceedings. i would also like to reiterate my commitment to the need to establish an ambitious european criminal area based on a comprehensive approach. much remains to be done to combat crime in europe more effectively, and in strict compliance with our fundamental values.
in writing. the challenge for the european criminal justice system is therefore to ensure that it is carried out in a way that respects and guarantees fundamental rights. it is significant that the preamble to the charter of fundamental rights expressly refers to the area of 'freedom, security and justice', which is by its very nature particularly sensitive in terms of fundamental rights and freedoms. it is unnecessary to recall that the guarantee must be 'real' and not 'formal'. the deliberate creation of the european criminal area implies that judicial review of respect for fundamental rights in the union must be guaranteed. the importance of the european criminal area is now clear. this is a priority in the construction of europe, with a gradual emancipation from the conventional cooperation mechanisms. after promoting police and judicial cooperation to compensate for the disappearance of internal borders, the european union is now moving beyond this interstate cooperation towards the progressive construction of a homogeneous criminal area.

in writing. the conclusion of this agreement is an important step for the eu in its efforts to make global forest management more sustainable, to stop deforestation and forest degradation, and to promote systemic change in the forest sector by rewarding the efforts of law-abiding economic operators who source timber from legitimate and reliable suppliers and protecting them from unfair competition. however, this heritage is being threatened by the massive and unbridled destruction of tropical rainforest and carbon-rich peatlands for palm oil and paper production, making indonesia the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and a major contributor to climate change. the voluntary partnership agreement also introduces new standards for the management of indonesian forests. however, it should be recalled that only approximately 10%[nbsp ]% in value of indonesian timber and timber products exports are currently destined for the european market, while the rest is mainly exported to asian countries.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, for over fifty years europe has been leading the efforts towards gender equality. i am very proud of the substantial progress which has been achieved during those years – and also since this commission took office – with the constant support of parliament. i think the report which has just been explained by madam zuber is a testimony to the way parliament has always taken the lead in advancing the cause of women. we have come a long way, but we still need to reduce many obstacles which women are facing in their private, public and economic lives. last year, in the framework of the europe 2020 strategy for growth, the commission addressed recommendations to 13 member states aimed at promoting female employment. the commission recommended that these member states invest in childcare facilities and remove fiscal disincentives for second earners. in addition, the eu provides significant co-funding possibilities in order to help member states to promote gender equality, notably through the european structural and investment funds. perhaps the most manifest form of gender inequality – and here i agree absolutely with madam zuber – is the gender pay gap, which has barely decreased in recent years. women earn on average 16.4[nbsp ]% less than men, according to the latest figures. now this, we all know, has multiple causes: women are working in undervalued and underpaid sectors and occupations; women are under-represented in senior and leadership positions; and they unequally share the burden of family and domestic responsibilities. other reasons, of course, are old societal patterns which say that women are not considered breadwinners by their employers, or simply the lack of information available to female employees. this is unacceptable, and we have to act. the commission has been consistently striving for equal pay to become a reality – be it by awareness-raising activities or by monitoring the application and enforcement of legislation on equal pay by the member states. last week, the commission provided member states with a toolbox of concrete measures to tackle pay discrimination and the persisting gender pay gap in the form of a non-binding legal act. we adopted a recommendation on strengthening the principle of equal pay between men and women through increased transparency. the first of its kind at eu level, this recommendation is a breakthrough, because more wage transparency could create further pressure for pay equality. the knowledge of different pay levels within a company or an industry is a powerful driver of change, and that knowledge is all too often missing today. this toolbox of measures builds on current best practices in the member states and will assist social partners and national authorities to take concrete steps towards reducing the gender pay gap. we should definitely continue to emphasise the economic reasoning against the gender pay gap and convince the overwhelmingly masculine business community that equality pays off. women are still facing barriers to advancement into senior management positions. today, they account for an average of 18[nbsp ]% of the members of boards of directors in the largest publicly-listed companies. this is up from 12[nbsp ]% three years earlier. we have witnessed a real talent hunt in recent years, as companies started to hire more women for top senior positions in 2010, when the commission first announced that it would consider targeted initiatives to improve gender diversity in companies. however, recent progress has not been evenly spread across the eu. most of the significant improvements took place in countries which have taken or have considered taking legislative action. as a consequence, the commission adopted the proposed directive for women on boards – you all know this directive – and i am very grateful for parliament’s support, as expressed in your first reading position. i really hope that the current blocking minority in the council can be overcome. the commission will continue to work constructively with co-legislators with a view to the speedy adoption of this landmark proposal. madam president, last week the fundamental rights agency released the first ever european survey on violence against women in order to help us to understand the extent of the problem. you all know that the figures are alarming. you have called on the commission to oppose violence against women, and we have responded. together, we have put in place a comprehensive legal framework at european level to protect women against all forms of violence. this framework includes the directive on trafficking in human beings, the directive against the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, the directive on the european protection order applicable in criminal matters, the regulation setting the european protection order covering the civil matters and, last but not least, the directive on the rights of crime victims, stressing the need for specific and appropriate protection for victims of gender-based violence. the european commission also adopted a comprehensive policy package against female genital mutilation in november[nbsp ]2013. it co-funded, in this context, 14 national governments’ campaigns against gender-based violence, as well as projects led by non-governmental organisations. madam president, honourable members, we all know that it is only by uniting forces and by everybody taking their responsibility – at european level, at national level, at local level and at the level of the ngos – that we can change things. we have to put our finger on the problem; we have to offer solutions to the problem. this we have done together in recent years, and i thank parliament for its very constructive and forward-looking actions. i also thank it for having really advanced the cause of women over the last few years.

in writing. i support the overall objective of the proposed regulation, which is to strengthen the economic governance of the union by establishing a strengthened system of statistical control of data relevant for the purposes of the mff. i recognise the need for clear requirements and procedures to ensure the optimum quality of statistics, with the aim of facilitating the early detection and monitoring of macroeconomic imbalances. however, your rapporteur believes that the monitoring of the statistical quality of the data relevant for the purposes of the mdp and of the reference statistical information could be better aligned with the framework defined in the macroeconomic imbalances procedure and with the legislation, practices and governance structures in place in the field of european statistics.
in writing. i voted in favour of the draft council decision on the renewal of the agreement for scientific and technological cooperation between the european community and the government of the united states of america.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report on access to genetic resources (nagoya protocol). as we know, biodiversity is an essential data for scientific research, technological applications, health products, food and cosmetics. unfortunately, for several decades now, this biodiversity has been seriously degraded. the report therefore proposes a series of measures to safeguard these resources, both biological and cultural: ensuring the integrity of the chain of use so that contracts concluded upstream of the exploitation of resources are clearly respected, banning 'biopiracy' in europe - in other words, the prohibition of the illegal acquisition and use of genetic resources - or, in order to safeguard global biodiversity, the creation of a fund on benefit-sharing. these measures are in the right direction and i have therefore voted in favour of this text.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by my colleague sandrine bélier on the draft council decision on the conclusion, on behalf of the european union, of the nagoya protocol on access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilization relating to the convention on biological diversity.
in writing. i voted in favour of the text by my distinguished colleague, mr frederic daerden. the spanish authorities state that 11,5% of all spanish enterprises are established in the comunidad valenciana, the nuts ii region concerned by the redundancies. the manufacturing sector accounts for 26% of jobs in this region, the services sector for 60%, the construction sector for 10%, and the primary sector for 4%. the economic model of the comunidad valenciana is characterised by a high proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises, mainly specialised in the manufacture of furniture, footwear, textiles, ceramics and toys. these industries are concentrated around a small number of municipalities. it is argued that the redundancies in the textile sector in the comunidad valenciana will only worsen the unemployment situation, since the region - in particular alicante, a nuts iii region - is highly dependent on this sector. of all the workers in the manufacturing industry in alicante, 8.24% are employed in the textile sector.
in writing. if a text is bad, it should be rejected. this is the best explanation for the massive vote this afternoon in the european parliament against the commission's proposal for a regulation on seeds. the vote was not surprising, given the number of critics, and it confirmed the opposite views already expressed by the parliament's agriculture and environment committees. it is no coincidence that a large number of citizens who are gardeners have written to me expressing their concern about a text which would significantly limit their access to a wide variety of seeds. the european commission certainly has better things to do than to submit legislation that citizens do not want because it is unnecessary and prescriptive. like the rapporteur, paolo silvestris, i am critical of a text which merges twelve directives into one regulation, which has not been the subject of any impact study on smes in the agricultural sector, and above all whose philosophy is wrong: eu legislation on agricultural seeds must promote the maintenance of biodiversity in agriculture and horticulture, and not the other way around! the commission has every interest in not persisting in its error and must withdraw its proposal!
in writing. we voted to reject the seeds dossier and sent the text back to the european commission for re-writing. the draft directive was a major threat to ancient seeds, thus putting european biodiversity at great risk, and it was a game played by a few large groups to the detriment of small farmers. it is not the lobbies of the big multinationals that decide the agenda. the big seed companies in the global marketplace are lobbying government officials and lawmakers to keep this niche market as small as possible and not to hinder their profits. these lobbies wanted the reform to be passed in force to avoid democratic debate because the original version of the text is clearly in their favour, serves the interests of small farmers and harms the maintenance of biodiversity!

in writing. the eu regulatory framework needs to evolve and adapt to these changes, which call for greater concern for the effectiveness of anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing arrangements, greater clarity and coherence in member states' regulations, and an extension of the scope of legislation to new threats and vulnerabilities. in the political and economic context of the crisis, it is all the more imperative to ensure that criminal activities do not exacerbate the problems that are arising and do not pose an additional threat to the implementation of genuine european solidarity and to the efforts to achieve a lasting and complete recovery.
in writing. - with the extension of the current anti-money laundering rules that we have approved today, we are ensuring that online gambling companies will also have to take measures in the future to prevent money laundering. the new rules require online gambling companies to conduct a customer survey whenever winnings exceed eur 2 000. this will increase transparency about gamblers who win remarkably large sums. a risk analysis should also be carried out on which gambling services are most vulnerable to money laundering. the new rules are therefore a good thing for sport, as sports betting is now also targeted by the anti-money laundering rules. this is how we prevent black money from being laundered through bribe-taking and illegal gambling. the new rules require gambling companies to alert the anti-money laundering unit if there is any suspicion that the money wagered is from a criminal source. in this way, the sports world becomes less vulnerable to the money laundering of criminals who bet on sports events.
in writing. the new directive aims to improve the current framework to prevent the financial system from being used to convert the proceeds of criminal activities into lawful funds. the commission proposal was drawn up following the commission's review of the implementation of the current directive and to reflect changes to the non-binding recommendations made by the financial action task force (fatf). the international monetary fund estimates that money laundering is widespread, amounting to almost 5% of world gdp. such criminal activities undermine the integrity of the financial sector, cause a loss of revenue for governments, distort competition, hinder the proper functioning of markets and undermine development.
in writing. i draw attention to the fact that the union will significantly reduce its investments in the balkans, the eastern partnership countries and north africa. the decline in investment is the result of long-term cuts in the union budget, which will affect all union policies. in the next budget period, the financial constraints will include a reduction in the eib's annual external lending budget from an average of eur 4.2 billion to eur 3.6 billion per year, affecting all the institution's activities.
in writing. i consider it essential that users take the necessary steps to obtain an access and benefit-sharing contract in the event of reuse of any genetic resource. i do, however, recognize the impossibility of tracing the origin of certain genetic resources, such as those acquired outside national jurisdictions and those known as 'historical'. in order to respond to this situation, i propose the creation of a european union benefit-sharing fund to be funded by the users of genetic resources with a view to preserving global biodiversity. the fund may eventually contribute to a global multilateral benefit-sharing mechanism as set out in article 10 of the nagoya protocol.
in writing. - with this agreement on car inspection, we have also given the green light to tackle fraud with odometers within the eu. as more and more second-hand cars are sold across borders, a european approach is needed. studies show that odometer fraud is more common when vehicles are sold abroad. the fact that there is no exchange of information between member states makes it very difficult to trace the history of a car. a european information exchange system should better protect consumers and increase road safety. the agreement obliges all member states to record mileage at car inspections so that this information can be exchanged within a new european information exchange system. in belgium, all mileage is tracked and checked via the car pass system. we hope that now we can quickly work on linking the different national information systems to avoid fraud with odometers, also across borders.
in writing. - the main vehicle inspections are among the minimum requirements for improving road safety. it is particularly important to me that existing stricter rules in the member states, such as the control system in belgium, should be maintained. the testing of motorcycles over 125ccm will be carried out from 2022 in the 12 countries where these checks are not currently carried out. however, member states are free to provide statistical evidence that they have introduced other measures to improve road safety for motorcycles. finally, i welcome the possible introduction of a 'car pass' which will prevent the manipulation of mileage.
in writing. the increased mobility of people within the european union requires more harmonised legislation on technical controls. it is necessary not only to improve road safety but also to give citizens valid information about vehicles purchased in another member state. as technology evolves, the legislation should be adjusted to include vehicles which, until now, were not covered by its scope.
in writing. this proposal, as part of the 'technical inspection' package, aims to promote and enforce the rules on the technical inspection of motor vehicles in order to enhance road safety and environmental protection. the aim of the directive is to improve the application of the rules on roadworthiness and roadworthiness tests, particularly where the technical condition of a vehicle poses a direct and immediate danger to road safety, by introducing measures such as temporary suspension or permanent cancellation of the vehicle's registration.
in writing. in the context of technical and roadworthiness tests, a large amount of data relating to the vehicle and its performance is collected. these data can be used by the various authorities to monitor the detection of defects and to organise targeted controls, but also to define more appropriate policies. similarly, road and technical inspections would be more effective if they had access to complete information on the vehicle's history and technical characteristics.
in writing. i think that the task of collecting accident data should not be taken away from eurostat. instead, cooperation with the european railway agency should be established and ensured in the area of data collection. in addition, a requirement concerning the collection of incident data should be added, as these contribute to improving the level of railway safety.

on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, this is in fact the last meeting of the european council before the elections, and i think it is a good moment to make an assessment of the last five years – of what has been done, what has not been done, and what the results of our policies have been. first of all let me say that over the last five years we had a very dramatic period, mr[nbsp ]barroso. we had the fallout from the financial crisis of 2008. we had the sovereign debt crisis that started in greece in december 2009. we had the arab spring in our neighbourhood. with our american friends we had the spying affair that is still going on and in connection with which we have to make new legislation as fast as possible. and now we have the deep crisis in the crimea, which reminds us of all the old tensions of the cold war. so the last five years has been a turbulent period. i think we also have to be honest about the fact that a number of things have been done. since the financial crisis in 2008, a huge new financial regulation based on initiatives by commissioner barnier has been put forward. we now have directives on bank recovery and resolution. we have a directive on the deposit guarantee schemes. we have a directive on markets in financial instruments. we have a directive on market abuse. we have a regulation on credit rating agencies and one on capital requirements. so a lot has been done on financial regulation. thanks to our colleague commissioner rehn, a lot has also been done on the rules of the growth and stability pact. and finally the rules are being applied; that was not always the case in the past. the last element is that we also have positive action by the european central bank. let us be honest, it is thanks to mr draghi’s omt that the tensions in the markets have fallen; unfortunately the tensions and the pressures on politicians to make the necessary reforms have also fallen. having said that, i think it is also necessary to tell the people – the citizens of europe – the truth. the crisis is not over. just because the end of the recession is here, this does not mean that we now have entered a period of growth – we have entered into a period of what we can more or less call economic stagnation, a goal between 0[nbsp ]% and 2[nbsp ]%. that is growth, but not enough to lower the enormous unemployment figures that we are experiencing in europe. and why? because i think we lack two elements. it was interesting that mr swoboda made a comparison between the us and the european result. why the difference? because, first of all, they have solved their banking problem and we are still in the middle of a banking crisis. we have still not created a system that is capable of transferring the money from the banks to the real economy: that is the problem. a small or medium-sized company in greece, for example, is still faced with interest rates of 7[nbsp ]%, 8[nbsp ]%, 9[nbsp ]% or 10[nbsp ]% for making investments, and the same is true for a small company in italy. we will not recover if we do not first of all create a banking union, and i am doubtful about the outcome of the trilogue today when i see what the council and ecofin decided yesterday – if they decided anything, because that is not very clear. the second thing we need is a european convergence policy. we need a new economic strategy. the lisbon agenda failed, the 2020 agenda failed. why? because it was not binding enough. if you have one currency you also need more convergence and more binding economic strategies between the different parts of your union. my last point – on a totally different matter – is that i think over the last five years we have seen a lack of unity in our foreign policy, and we are seeing it today again in the crisis in ukraine and the crimea. an outrageous lack of courage on the part of the european union, because it is our neighbourhood: we are talking about ukraine, which is in fact a european country. when you go to odessa or kiev you see that you are in the middle of europe – and what are we doing? what is our attitude to the tragedy that is happening in the crimea? there is no serious strategy at all, and we need one. in my opinion we need one based on a number of elements. first of all, a real common energy policy and, as graham watson indicated, we need binding targets. it is the only way to have a real common energy policy. we also need to launch real sanctions against russia, against the dirty money coming from russia and which is invested in german industry, in the city of london, in real estate in france. we need real sanctions, otherwise the case is over. crimea becomes a new frozen conflict for years and for decades. so let us be clear: we are dealing with a russian leadership that has turned its back on the consensus following the cold war. it is no longer the russian leadership of 1990 and the years after. it is a russian leadership which is no longer prepared to accept the integrity of its former parts. it started, as we know, in 2008 in georgia and it is continuing now in the crimea, and the only way to stop it is by being bold, by being courageous in the european union and doing what is necessary.
in writing. the union's energy policy is only relevant in the context of a transversal industrial policy conducive to economic recovery. the main lines of this european industrial policy, which should be pursued at all levels of government, would be: an aggressive trade policy; the adjustment of the rules on state aid and their notification thresholds; massive investment in r&d and training, which is difficult to reconcile with the current austerity imposed on the european and national budgets; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this reduction is through environmental efforts, such as increasing the share of renewable energy or our energy efficiency. yes, europe must set the example in this respect worldwide, with binding standards and strengthened objectives, but accompanied by a fair trade policy which is demanding in environmental and social matters. otherwise, it cannot fight alone, without first having implemented a binding international agreement. recent layoffs in the steel, automotive, glass and high-tech industries support my point. in short, an energy and environmental ambition in the service of reindustrialisation.
the european commission states that the european economy is recovering and that the economic outlook is favourable. although i welcome this statement, i cannot help but be critical of it. the growth in question is very minimal: 0,1% in the euro area between january 2013 and january 2014. no real progress was made in the area of unemployment: in both january 2013 and january 2014, it was 12% in the euro area. this result is very surprising when you compare it with the efforts made in many member states. i would also like to stress once again that the social cost of the crisis measures imposed by the troika is enormous. the damage caused by the breakdown of the social system will be felt for years to come. it is therefore essential that the social dimension of emu be developed further. it should be clear by now that economic policy must be balanced with social policy. this is the only way to achieve the social revival of europe. i therefore ask the council to pay sufficient attention to the social dimension at its meeting on 21 and 22 march. because we need a different policy.
the crisis, ladies and gentlemen, shows that there is a need to upgrade european foreign policy, to upgrade security and defence policy. if we don't, we'll always be late or we'll react too weakly. putin knows that and he can go about his business. for him, a democratic revolution in ukraine is a nightmare. and so he's distracting attention from that at home by invading abroad. and unfortunately it is the citizens of ukraine who feel this. and it's going from bad to worse. in crimea journalists and activists are disappearing, citizens are being pressured in the run-up to the so-called referendum, crimean tatars are being threatened. in eastern ukraine, russian sabotage groups are at work. that is a matter of grave concern to us. we support the measures taken by the council and the commission. the best course of action we can take is to invest in the success of the ukrainian democratic revolution. the european parliament has been a key player in the consolidation of the pro-european vote. that's putin's greatest fear, and he's not going to let that happen. only then can the limited diplomatic and sanctions measures succeed.

in writing. the european fisheries sector faces several challenges: the catch sector is faced with rising fuel costs, labour shortages and quota restrictions. the processing sector suffers from constraints in the supply of raw materials and competition from imports from third countries. the aquaculture sector also faces competition from imports, low prices for certain species, strict environmental regulations and conflicts over land use. the current situation of the european fisheries sector is seriously weakening its competitive position, especially as the world market is being liberalized and as some developing countries with abundant marine resources are beginning to become the new powers in the fisheries sector. the survival of the european fisheries sector will be jeopardised if the european union liberalises trade in fishery products with developing countries wishing to export their products to the interesting european market, especially if it grants a zero duty.
in writing. food plays a fundamental role in societies. while nutrition and access to clean water remain pressing problems for many developing countries, our countries are facing other problems in this area. these are diseases and pathologies (obesity, anorexia, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, etc.) which entail significant costs for health systems, both public and private. in order to minimise these costs, this report also stresses the importance of integrating the teaching of healthy eating and nutrition into our national education programmes. in addition to promoting good practice, these programmes could also help to develop and promote our territories in order to develop tourism. i therefore voted in favour of this report, which proposes the implementation of genuine european public policies in the field of food and gastronomy.
in writing. developments in recent years have highlighted the extraordinary importance of food, in the broad sense, in today's society. on the one hand, in the context of the millennium development goals, major efforts are needed to eradicate hunger and the problems of drinking water supply in all countries still suffering from this scourge of humanity, which is absolutely unacceptable in the 21st century. on the other hand, it is surprising that in developed countries with a good economic level, due to lack of culture and/or education, diet has become a fundamental cause of diseases and pathologies that entail considerable costs for the public or private health system. in fact, poor diet is a major cause of obesity, anorexia, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and stomach problems, among others. of course, the problem is not just poor nutrition. for all these conditions, lack of physical exercise, the ingestion of harmful substances, such as drugs, excessive alcohol and tobacco, and problems with emotional balance also play a major role.
in writing. the legislation on the protection of personal data in the union was voted on wednesday. the citizen finally in control of his personal data: it sounds like a dream that should have always remained a reality. explicit consent of the internet user for the information he leaves on the web, limitation of profiling, prohibition for google, facebook or skype to transfer data to third countries without a european agreement and heavy sanctions against platforms that would violate the rules: real firewalls protecting the rights of the european citizen are put in place. twenty years ago, the internet was the exception, now it's the rule, from 16 million to 2.7 billion internet users worldwide. the network has spread and the stakes have become economic. for a long time, people thought that surfing was free, but they were paying, unknowingly, by giving up their personal data. the value of personal data is now estimated at over 300 billion euros. new legislation was needed.

in writing. the european union's relations with the republic of azerbaijan began in 1996 with the signing of the partnership and cooperation agreement (pca). later, following the 2004 and 2007 enlargements, the european union launched the european neighbourhood policy, in which the republic of azerbaijan has participated since 2004 and which aims to strengthen relations with the countries neighbouring it to the east and south, in order to promote prosperity, stability and security on the borders of the union. in 2009, the european union launched a new initiative in this direction, aimed at deepening relations with certain eastern countries: the eastern partnership. an association agreement was concluded in prague on 7 may 2009 to which the republic of azerbaijan is also a party. the aim of this partnership is to create the conditions necessary to accelerate political association and economic integration between the european union and the participating states. visa liberalisation and citizens' mobility are an integral part of this partnership.

in writing. - european airspace needs to be more efficient. the achievement of the 'single european sky' requires a major overhaul. there are 27,000 flights across europe every day. a fragmented approach threatens to saturate european airspace, with a number of negative consequences: loss of competitiveness, delays, increased fuel consumption and emissions. the current fragmentation is estimated to cost as much as 5 billion euros a year. efficiency is a must and benefits all actors involved: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on competition are applied in a fair and transparent manner. by managing our airspace wisely, we can reduce costs and emissions while leaving enough capacity. in addition, the proposed flexibility for the functional airspace blocks (fabs) is of great importance. this will allow us to achieve results more quickly, for example at benelux level, to the benefit of all the players in the sector. it's getting a lot more chances now.
written. - the existing fragmentation of european airspace is based on the fact that there are 28 different national aviation authorities with over 100 different air traffic control service providers and different systems and procedures. this fragmentation will add approximately eur 5 billion to the cost of flights and will extend the average duration of flights in european airspace by 42 km. however, due to a lack of willingness on the part of member states, cross-border functional airspace blocks have still not been implemented, despite having been decided in single european sky i in 2004 and ii in 2009. this is why this single european sky ii+ (ses[nbsp ]ii+) package was put together, which is intended, among other things, to accelerate the reform of the air safety services. but even this ses ii+ will not have much effect if the member states are not finally ready to put the promised cooperation into practice.
in writing. the single european sky (ses) initiative, launched in 2000, extended the common transport policy to air traffic management and air navigation services. since then, the european air transport market has expanded to include no less than 38 countries, as a result of the enlargement policy, combined with an active neighbourhood policy, so that it is now a global player. the fact remains that the cue did not meet expectations. the bottom-up approach of functional airspace blocks has made little progress, while the overall efficiency of the configuration and management of the european road network has improved little. the considerable reduction in shipping charges, ticket prices, average flight times or fuel consumption that the ongoing reform of the ceu was expected to bring about was not sufficient. airspace users and passengers are therefore paying for the shortcomings in the european air transport chain: wasted time, unnecessary fuel consumption and costs that could be avoided.
in writing. this is a very important regulation for two reasons: firstly, to adapt to the new rules of the single european sky; secondly, to reform governance to implement the interinstitutional agreement on european agencies concluded in july 2012. in this agreement, the commission, the european parliament and the council agreed on a common approach to european agencies. the agreement, while not legally binding, is based on a common, case-by-case approach and brings progress on a wide range of issues (establishment, choice of seat, governance, operation, use of resources and control arrangements for the agencies).
in writing. - this report is important because it adapts the package travel directive, which has been in force since 1990, to the present age of the internet. package holidays are increasingly booked via the internet. however, in addition to providing several services, such as transport and accommodation, package holidays often involve several companies, such as tour operators, cruise lines, airlines, etc. the consumer is becoming increasingly confused as to whom to turn to in the event of problems and who bears what responsibility. the aim of this report is to eliminate these ambiguities. the commission has also proposed to amend the definition of 'package travel' to include 'package travel' as defined in the package travel directive. this will enable the consumer to identify which trip he is benefiting from the information obligation, liability and insolvency protection provisions of the eu package travel directive. i also welcome the fact that consumer rights are being strengthened by the introduction of eligibility criteria which tour operators must comply with in the event of a price increase. for example, the price increase may not exceed 8% of the price of the package.

in writing. the new european copernicus 2014-2020 programme (which replaces the existing gmes) provides europe with continuous, independent and reliable access to earth observation data and information. this data will be collected by satellites and a network of sensors on land, at sea and in the air. the copernicus system will enable europe to better manage the environment and its natural resources, agriculture, various pollution, climate change, natural and man-made disasters, civil protection, security, etc. i voted in favour of copernicus, with a budget of eur 3.79 billion over 7 years, for reasons of centralised and coherent operation at european level with effects that will be felt by all citizens. the second, equally important reason for my vote in favour is the economic impact of the regional level. it is estimated that this could generate €30 billion and create 50 000 new european jobs between 2015 and 2030. i am thinking more specifically of the positive effects for smes, research centres and innovative companies in the aeronautics and space sector in the liège region.
in writing. through an appropriate data policy, copernicus can boost europe's earth observation services and user services sector, helping them to become a world leader. the policy of full, open and free access to data is an important part of the copernicus regulation, as in principle europeans should not pay twice for the same data. however, an appropriate data policy must take into account strategic and economic considerations and not harm the competitiveness of european industries. in terms of access to data, reciprocity with third countries not contributing to the programme is an important means of ensuring fair competition. exceptions to this principle should be provided for in emergency situations and situations involving civil security, or where added value is envisaged for other european policies, in particular for development aid activities. the commission's negotiation of agreements with third countries on other matters is already provided for in the regulation, which facilitates the integration of this principle.

in writing. convergence means the merging of audiovisual media services, linear and non-linear, which were considered to be largely separate from each other until now. the traditional media are being joined by new providers from the telecommunications industry, but also by over-the-top (ott) operators. the system of tiered regulation of the sma directive has so far ensured that a certain minimum standard is met in europe for conventional (linear) television content and for non-linear television media or online offers. the digitisation of broadcasting and media technologies, the convergence of technical transmission channels and the continuous evolution of mobile and hybrid devices mean that, on the same screen, traditional, regulated broadcasting and consultation services are suddenly faced with competition from hitherto unregulated content from the open internet. this raises questions about the protection of consumers, young people and data, but also about the preservation of diversity and the dual cultural and economic character of the media.

we don't think so, not in our opinion. it is true that we can say that economic and monetary union has not broken down, but it is still wobbling, and i would like to say to some colleagues that there is no monetary union that can survive without financial transfers from one part of the union to another. there is no historical or current example of monetary union without a strong federal budget, without financial transfers. you may like it or not, this is the reality, but no sustainable solution has been found so far. it is true that some member states have regained access to the financial markets, but you will allow me not to judge the quality and prosperity of a country by the judgment of the financial markets. the question is therefore: at what cost have we saved economic and monetary union so far? the price, ladies and gentlemen, is growth. the growth of debt, public and private, the growth of inequality, the growth of unemployment, the growth of emigration, the growth of poverty and insecurity, the growth of infant mortality. i would remind you that several million greeks no longer have access to health care. so if the crisis is the result of an irresponsible level of debt -- and i agree with those who say this -- it's as much irresponsible public debt in greece as it is irresponsible private debt in the financial and real estate bubble countries of spain and ireland. there is no irresponsible debt without irresponsible borrowers on one side of the table and irresponsible lenders on the other. the troika has systematically favoured the protection of creditors against debtors, so that today it is the most vulnerable people who pay the price of adjustment, as they say. all these choices were made outside any democratic control. i have heard the commission tell us that democratic control was formally in place. what i find is that when you negotiate with a gun to your head, you can't say that your choices are free. similarly, those in the eurogroup who approved the aid plans for the various countries did so without obtaining any mandate from their own parliaments. so, both in terms of the policies that are being implemented and in terms of democratic control, there is a revolution to be made in the way the european union comes to the rescue of its member states. i shall stop here, since i see that my speaking time is up.
